title: VW cars could be eavesdropped on and tracked via Bluetooth for 16 months
excerpt: After 16 months, VW fixes a security flaw in hundreds of thousands of cars. A demonstration showed how to tap the microphone and track a VW ID.4.
content_html:
Turn up the heat, track the route and listen in on conversations during the drive: IT researchers at Hungarian cybersecurity firm PCA Cyber Security have shown that cockpit functions in VW cars can still be hijacked over Bluetooth. The attack exploits a vulnerability the researchers reported to automakers in 2024 and disclosed about a year and a half ago.

The security researchers estimate that several hundred thousand cars made by the German automaker are affected. That’s according to a report by the British daily newspaper “The Times.” The PCA security team reportedly demonstrated to the newspaper’s journalists in Budapest how attackers can hijack an ID.4’s entertainment system after pairing over Bluetooth. The attack made it possible to tap the hands-free microphone to listen in, track the vehicle’s location via GPS and control features such as the heater, windshield wipers and sunroof from a laptop outside the car.

But how is this possible? The vulnerability known as “PerfektBlue”, a collection of flaws in the BlueSDK Bluetooth stack, has been known for about a year and a half. The flaw allows attackers to inject malicious code wirelessly after an approved Bluetooth pairing and gain admin privileges over car functions accessible through the infotainment system. PCA published details of the attack chain in a security advisory on PerfektBlue.

Asked why the automaker is only now starting to patch the flaw, VW said it had quickly fixed the vulnerability in ID. models running software newer than version 5.0. Fixing it took longer in models with older software because “the already planned integrated management system had to be modified, and new security processes then had to be carried out.”

Update has been rolling out to VW drivers for several weeks

A VW spokesperson told heise online on Thursday: “Volkswagen thoroughly investigated the reported vulnerabilities in the infotainment system.” The problem affects an older generation of infotainment systems, which apparently are no longer installed in current electric cars such as the ID. Polo. The spokesperson clarified that the vulnerability does not affect driving safety because attackers cannot access functions such as the steering, brakes or accelerator. “At no time has there been, or is there now, any danger to the safety of our customers or our vehicles.”

The VW spokesperson nevertheless advises customers to “never accept an unknown Bluetooth pairing request” or connect unknown USB devices to their cars. That helps because a successful attack requires the driver to accept the Bluetooth connection. So if a suspicious pairing request appears on the display, drivers should think carefully about whether to accept it. If they decline, attackers cannot access the infotainment system.

The automaker says it has only been making an update available for about three weeks. Software version 3.9.1 patches the flaw in cars running a version older than 4.0. The update can be installed over the air, via cellular or Wi-Fi while the car is parked. Owners of cars running a version newer than 4.0 have to take them to a repair shop to install the update. According to VW, cars running software version 5.6 or later are not affected. Drivers should check with VW if they are unsure whether an update is recommended. No recall is planned.
